paragraphs: Statistical analysis commonly starts by deciding what kind of variable each dataset column represents. A variable might describe an unordered category, an ordered category, or a real-valued measurement. Those choices affect how a model interprets observations and represents noise. This paper treats those choices as something to learn from the data.

The motivation is practical: real datasets often mix different kinds of variables and arrive with incomplete or unreliable documentation. Assuming that their statistical types and suitable likelihood models are already known can therefore be restrictive. The authors propose a Bayesian method to address the discovery of these modeling ingredients automatically.

The reported results show accurate identification of statistical data types on both synthetic and real datasets. The contribution is a way to support a decision that usually precedes model fitting but is often taken for granted. By making variable interpretation part of inference, the approach addresses uncertainty about how heterogeneous data should be modeled.
icml-2017-automatic-discovery-of-the-sta.tldr: A Bayesian method automatically identifies statistical variable types in heterogeneous, incompletely documented datasets.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good inputs to a black-box function by learning from previous evaluations. With many input dimensions, both the learning problem and the computations become difficult. This paper addresses those obstacles through two coordinated choices: learning structure within the function and evaluating several candidate inputs in parallel.

The structural assumption is that the function has a hidden additive organization, so its behavior can be represented through contributions that add together. The method infers this organization using Gibbs sampling. This matters because the decomposition is learned rather than supplied in advance, allowing the optimization procedure to use the structure it discovers.

The method also uses determinantal point processes to construct batches of evaluation queries. Parallel evaluations are intended to reduce the number of optimization iterations required. Experiments on synthetic and real-world functions report better performance than the existing approaches considered. These findings support combining learned additive structure with batched evaluation for the high-dimensional optimization problems studied.
icml-2017-batched-high-dimensional-bayes.tldr: Learning hidden additive structure and choosing parallel evaluation batches improves Bayesian optimization on the high-dimensional functions studied.

paragraphs: Block Gauss-Seidel updates groups of coordinates while solving an optimization problem. Momentum can accelerate this procedure, but earlier analysis considered coordinate groups fixed before optimization begins. This paper asks whether that grouping choice itself restricts performance, even when the updates within those groups use an accelerated method.

The authors construct instances where ordinary Gauss-Seidel with randomly sampled coordinates substantially outperforms accelerated Gauss-Seidel under every fixed partition. This establishes that acceleration alone does not resolve the disadvantages of fixed groups in those instances. It motivates analyzing an accelerated algorithm that also samples coordinates randomly, combining the two sources of improvement.

The resulting analysis describes acceleration through a new parameter that depends on the data and behaves well when matrix sub-blocks are well-conditioned. Experiments on large machine learning tasks report speedups over non-accelerated Gauss-Seidel and conjugate gradients. Together, the construction and experiments show why coordinate selection deserves attention alongside the choice of acceleration mechanism.
icml-2017-breaking-locality-accelerates-.tldr: Random coordinate sampling can overcome fixed-block bottlenecks and make accelerated Gauss-Seidel faster on the tasks studied.

paragraphs: Graph diffusion repeatedly spreads mass between connected vertices, making it useful for discovering clusters. However, spreading too freely can move mass outside the cluster a procedure is meant to identify. This paper introduces Capacity Releasing Diffusion, a process described as faster and more local than classical spectral diffusion.

The authors use this process to build a local graph clustering algorithm. Its guarantee applies when diffusion starts inside a cluster whose vertices are better connected internally than externally by an O(log² n) factor, with n denoting the cluster size. Under the stated conditions, the algorithm avoids the quadratic Cheeger barrier that constrains traditional local clustering guarantees.

The theoretical result also requires a smoothness condition. The authors suspect this condition comes from their analysis, but do not establish that it can be removed. Empirical results show improvements, particularly on realistic social graphs containing moderately strong clusters. The contribution therefore combines a locality-focused diffusion process with a conditional theoretical improvement and supporting experiments.
icml-2017-capacity-releasing-diffusion-f.tldr: Capacity Releasing Diffusion improves local graph clustering, with a guarantee beyond the quadratic Cheeger barrier under stated connectivity and smoothness conditions.

paragraphs: Distributed sparse learning fits a model using observations held across multiple machines, while favoring solutions with relatively few active coefficients. The central question here is whether those machines can reach the statistical accuracy of a centralized method without requiring many rounds of communication. The paper studies observations randomly partitioned across machines.

Each round divides the work between workers and a master. Workers compute loss gradients using their local observations. The master then solves a shifted loss minimization problem with an ℓ1 penalty, which promotes sparsity. This arrangement combines information from local datasets through gradient computations and an updated optimization problem at the master.

The authors prove that the method matches the estimation error bound of centralized approaches after a number of communication rounds growing only logarithmically with the number of machines. That round count is independent of the other problem parameters in the stated result. The finding connects distributed computation with centralized statistical accuracy under the random-partition setting considered.
icml-2017-efficient-distributed-learning.tldr: With randomly partitioned observations, a distributed sparse-learning method matches centralized error bounds after logarithmically many communication rounds.

paragraphs: The paper studies fitting linear predictors by minimizing empirical risk with convex losses. These objectives can be rewritten as saddle point problems and addressed with primal-dual first-order algorithms. Such algorithms often rely on an explicitly strongly convex regularizer to obtain linear convergence, a rate at which optimization error decreases geometrically.

The authors develop batch and randomized algorithms that adaptively exploit strong convexity arising from the data. This allows them to achieve linear convergence even without regularization when the relevant curvature is available. The distinction matters because useful curvature can already be present in the learning objective, rather than needing to be introduced through an additional penalty.

A second contribution addresses the dual proximal mapping, an update operation that may lack a simple formula or an efficient solution. The proposed dual-free variants avoid requiring that operation and are described as particularly suitable for logistic regression. Together, the contributions target both the source of fast convergence and a computational obstacle within primal-dual updates.
icml-2017-exploiting-strong-convexity-fr.tldr: Adaptive primal-dual algorithms use strong convexity supplied by data to enable linear convergence, with dual-free variants suited to logistic regression.

paragraphs: An intensity function describes how frequently events occur across a domain. A Cox process makes that intensity random, extending the Poisson process to include uncertainty in the event-generating rate itself. This paper develops fast Bayesian inference for the permanental process, where the square root of the intensity is modeled as a Gaussian process.

The approach uses connections with reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces to derive efficient approximate inference algorithms. It applies a Laplace approximation to the predictive distribution and marginal likelihood. These are central quantities for describing predictions and assessing the model through observed data, so computing them efficiently directly addresses the cost of Bayesian intensity estimation.

The authors obtain a simple algorithm and apply it to both toy examples and real-world problems. They report speed improvements of orders of magnitude over previous work. The result supports the computational value of this approximation scheme for the studied problems while retaining the permanental process as the underlying probabilistic model.
icml-2017-fast-bayesian-intensity-estima.tldr: Kernel-space connections and Laplace approximations make Bayesian permanental-process inference orders of magnitude faster in the reported applications.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning tasks can require actions now whose consequences become apparent much later. FeUdal Networks address this challenge by organizing decision-making into two levels that operate at different time scales. The architecture separates the learning roles of these levels, allowing longer-term direction and immediate action selection to develop within one framework.

A Manager operates relatively slowly and supplies abstract goals to a Worker. The Worker acts at every environment step, translating those goals into primitive actions. This separation supports assigning credit over long periods and encourages different sub-policies to emerge for different Manager goals. The hierarchy therefore links sustained objectives to the sequence of actions used to pursue them.

The authors report that this architecture dramatically outperforms a strong baseline on tasks involving long-term credit assignment or memorization. Those findings concern settings where retaining information or connecting delayed outcomes to earlier behavior is especially important. The contribution is a concrete architecture for learning and acting across multiple temporal resolutions.
icml-2017-feudal-networks-for-hierarchic.tldr: FeUdal Networks combine a slower goal-setting Manager with a step-by-step Worker to improve performance on long-horizon reinforcement learning tasks.

paragraphs: Clustering data from multiple subspaces becomes challenging when those subspaces occupy many of the available dimensions. Hyperplanes are a prominent example. Existing correctness guarantees for sparse and low-rank clustering methods assume relatively low-dimensional subspaces, while alternatives for hyperplanes can be computationally demanding or have insufficient theoretical support.

This paper extends Dual Principal Component Pursuit to data drawn from multiple hyperplanes. Its theoretical contribution gives conditions under which the associated nonconvex ℓ1 problem has a unique global minimizer equal to the normal vector of the most dominant hyperplane. A normal vector describes a hyperplane's orientation, so recovering it provides a route to identifying that component.

Motivated by this result, the authors propose both sequential, RANSAC-style algorithms and iterative, K-Hyperplanes-style algorithms. Experiments on synthetic and real data show performance that exceeds or is competitive with existing methods. The work connects a conditional recovery guarantee for one dominant hyperplane with practical procedures for learning several hyperplanes and clustering their data.
icml-2017-hyperplane-clustering-via-dual.tldr: Extending Dual Principal Component Pursuit yields conditional hyperplane recovery guarantees and competitive algorithms for clustering multiple hyperplanes.

paragraphs: A dynamic knowledge graph records relationships together with the times at which they occur. Reasoning over such a graph requires accounting for changes in entities and relationships over time. Know-Evolve addresses this by learning entity representations that evolve nonlinearly, rather than treating each entity's representation as fixed throughout the observed history.

The model connects these changing representations to a multivariate point process, which describes the occurrence of timestamped facts. A score computed from the entity embeddings modulates the intensity for a fact. This links the representation of a relationship to its temporal occurrence, bringing relational information and event timing into the same modeling framework.

On two large real-world datasets, the authors report significantly better performance than several relational learning approaches. They also report effective prediction of when a fact will occur or recur. This timing capability is presented as a new contribution relative to earlier multi-relational reasoning approaches, extending the task beyond identifying relationships to anticipating their occurrence.
icml-2017-know-evolve-deep-temporal-reas.tldr: Know-Evolve combines evolving entity embeddings with a point process to reason about relationships and predict when facts occur or recur.

paragraphs: Determinantal point processes are probabilistic models whose repulsive behavior makes them useful when an application needs a diverse set of objects. Efficient procedures already exist for sampling from these models and computing several related probabilities. This paper addresses a less understood problem: learning the model's parameters from observed data.

The authors establish the optimal sample complexity, describing the amount of data needed for learning. They show that this requirement is governed by a structural parameter they call cycle sparsity. This identifies a property of the learning problem that determines its statistical difficulty, connecting the data requirement to the structure being recovered.

They also provide a provably fast combinatorial algorithm that efficiently implements the method of moments and attains the optimal sample complexity. Experimental results support the theoretical findings. The combined contribution is both statistical and computational: it characterizes the achievable data requirement and supplies an efficient learning procedure that reaches that requirement.
icml-2017-learning-determinantal-point-p.tldr: Cycle sparsity governs optimal DPP learning sample complexity, which a fast combinatorial method-of-moments algorithm achieves.

paragraphs: Learning a dynamical system from data is useful when no model derived from physical principles is available. Yet an absence of detailed equations does not mean an absence of useful knowledge. This paper focuses on stability as a known behavioral property that should inform the learned model, especially for controller design or movement generation.

The proposed framework learns nonlinear stochastic systems in a state-dependent coefficient form. In this representation, coefficients vary with the system's state. The targeted models are globally asymptotically stable according to probabilistic Lyapunov methods, bringing a stability requirement into the identification problem while accounting for the stochastic nature of the dynamics.

The authors compare their approach with other methods on real-world datasets in terms of flexibility and stability. The stated contribution is a framework that incorporates behavioral knowledge into data-driven system identification. It connects learning from observations with a formal stability property relevant to how the resulting model will be used.
icml-2017-learning-stable-stochastic-non.tldr: A learning framework incorporates probabilistic stability requirements into the identification of nonlinear stochastic dynamical systems.

paragraphs: Predicting a video by repeatedly feeding generated frames back into a model can amplify small pixel errors over time. This paper separates prediction of the scene's high-level structure from generation of its visual appearance. The goal is to remove the feedback path through which errors in generated pixels propagate into later predictions.

The method first estimates structure from the input frames and then predicts how that structure evolves. It generates future frames using the predicted structure and a single observed past frame. An LSTM predicts the structural evolution, while an analogy-based convolutional encoder-decoder produces the images. Future image generation therefore does not require observing earlier pixel-level predictions.

The model is evaluated on long-term prediction of human actions using Human3.6M and Penn Action. The authors report significantly better results than existing leading methods. The architecture specifically prevents propagation through recursively observed generated frames; its contribution is to organize the prediction task around structure and appearance as separate components.
icml-2017-learning-to-generate-long-term.tldr: Predicting high-level structure before rendering future frames avoids recursive pixel-error propagation and improves long-term human-action video prediction.

paragraphs: Information-based Bayesian optimization chooses evaluations according to how much they are expected to reveal about an unknown function's optimum. Entropy Search and Predictive Entropy Search seek information about the input where the maximum occurs. Although empirically successful, their entropy calculations are expensive, making the selection of evaluations computationally burdensome.

Max-value Entropy Search changes the information target to the maximum function value itself. The distinction is between learning where the best point lies and learning how high the function can go. The authors relate this criterion to other Bayesian optimization methods and establish a regret bound, giving the proposal a theoretical connection to optimization performance.

Empirically, the method maintains or improves the performance of the earlier entropy-search methods while greatly reducing computation. It is also less sensitive to the number of samples used to estimate entropy. The reported robustness makes these calculations more efficient in higher-dimensional problems, where the cost of choosing an evaluation is especially consequential.
icml-2017-max-value-entropy-search-for-e.tldr: Max-value Entropy Search lowers Bayesian optimization overhead by seeking information about the best function value.

paragraphs: Influence maximization chooses initial users in a social network to make as many people as possible aware of a product. The challenge becomes harder when the marketer does not know how information spreads. This paper develops a parametrization designed to be statistically efficient to learn without committing to a particular underlying diffusion model.

The authors construct a monotone, submodular surrogate and show that it approximates the original influence objective well. They also study a marketer who must learn about propagation while choosing seed users. For this setting, they introduce pairwise-influence semi-bandit feedback and a LinUCB-based algorithm that combines learning with ongoing decisions.

Their analysis gives a regret bound with improved dependence on network size compared with previous work. Experiments suggest robustness across underlying diffusion models and efficient learning of a near-optimal solution. The contribution joins a model-independent representation of influence with an online learning procedure, addressing both what to optimize and how to learn while acting.
icml-2017-model-independent-online-learn.tldr: A model-independent influence framework learns seed-selection decisions online, with improved network-size dependence in its regret bound.

paragraphs: Extreme multilabel classification may involve thousands to millions of possible labels, even though each example has only a few relevant ones. This paper uses that sparsity to formulate prediction through group testing. The approach operates with binary outputs, allowing it to use established binary classifiers as its learning components.

The authors describe several constructions and advocate concatenated Reed Solomon codes and unbalanced bipartite expander graphs. Error-correcting structure plays a central role: errors in individual classifier predictions can be repaired when decoding the labels. The stated correction capability includes a linearly growing number of classifier errors, and the paper establishes Hamming loss bounds for the approach.

Prediction uses a simple algorithm that avoids matrix inversion and solving optimization problems, keeping that stage inexpensive. Experiments across several datasets report superior performance. The contribution combines sparse label structure, binary classification, and coding-based correction so that a large output space can be handled with efficient prediction and explicit protection against classifier mistakes.
icml-2017-multilabel-classification-with.tldr: Group testing and error-correcting codes enable inexpensive multilabel prediction with provable error control for sparse label vectors.

paragraphs: Learning long-term dependencies is difficult when gradients shrink or grow excessively during backpropagation. One proposed response is to encourage or enforce orthogonal weight matrices, whose transformations preserve gradient norms. This paper examines how that choice affects optimization, considering convergence, speed, and gradient stability together rather than treating norm preservation as sufficient evidence of better training.

The authors introduce a factorization and parametrization of weight matrices that lets them bound matrix norms. This provides control over how much the matrix transformations can expand signals during backpropagation. The parametrization serves as a way to investigate the effects of different degrees of constraint on the learning process.

The study finds that hard orthogonality constraints can reduce convergence speed and hurt model performance. This is a qualified finding about possible costs of strict constraints, not a claim that orthogonality is always harmful. Its significance is that a desirable property of gradient propagation can coexist with disadvantages for optimization and the resulting model.
icml-2017-on-orthogonality-and-learning-.tldr: Controlling recurrent weight-matrix norms reveals that strict orthogonality can slow convergence and reduce model performance.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a target decision policy would perform using observations collected by another policy. This paper studies contextual bandits in the general setting where no consistent reward model is available. It establishes a minimax lower bound on mean squared error, characterizing the best possible worst-case accuracy in that setting.

Inverse propensity scoring and doubly robust estimators match this bound up to constants. This means their worst-case behavior is already optimal at that level of precision. The result differs from settings such as multi-armed bandits or contextual bandits with a consistent reward model, where inverse propensity scoring is suboptimal.

The authors then introduce SWITCH, which can use an available reward model even if that model is not consistent. It aims for a better balance between bias and variance than the two established estimators. They prove an upper bound on its error and report benefits across diverse datasets, often with improvements of orders of magnitude over prior work.
icml-2017-optimal-and-adaptive-off-polic.tldr: The paper establishes worst-case off-policy evaluation limits and proposes SWITCH to improve the bias-variance tradeoff using an imperfect reward model.

paragraphs: Gaussian graphical models describe relationships between variables through a precision matrix, the inverse of a covariance matrix. This paper studies estimating a sparse precision matrix when the data are high-dimensional and can contain arbitrary corruption. Its aim is to recover the model reliably despite damaged observations.

The method builds on a robust covariance estimator based on truncated inner products. The authors establish guarantees for estimation error and model selection consistency. In particular, the robust estimator attains the standard estimator's statistical rate when the number of corrupted observations per variable is at most on the order of √n/√log d, where n is sample size and d is the variable count.

The arbitrary nature of the corruption therefore does not imply tolerance of an unrestricted amount: the stated rate guarantee has an explicit corruption bound. The paper also proposes hypothesis testing to assess estimation uncertainty. Experiments on synthetic and real genomic data demonstrate the method's effectiveness, complementing its estimation and model-selection guarantees.
icml-2017-robust-gaussian-graphical-mode.tldr: A robust covariance-based estimator recovers sparse Gaussian graphical models at the standard statistical rate under a stated bound on corruption.

paragraphs: Probabilistic models depend on assumptions about how observations arise. When real data depart from those assumptions, inference and prediction can deteriorate. This paper proposes a general way to detect and reduce such mismatch across a broad class of models by learning how strongly individual observations should influence the analysis.

The method raises each observation's likelihood contribution to a weight and infers these weights alongside the model's latent variables. Observations that fit the assumptions can retain influence, while others are down-weighted. This makes the treatment of mismatched observations part of Bayesian inference, allowing the model to adjust their contributions based on the data.

The authors investigate four forms of mismatch, including missing latent groups and incorrectly specified structure. They report robust inference and improved predictive accuracy, with a Poisson factorization analysis of Movielens 1M illustrating practical benefits. The contribution is a systematic reweighting mechanism that can reduce the effect of assumption violations without requiring each mismatch to be handled by a separate model redesign.
icml-2017-robust-probabilistic-modeling-.tldr: Bayesian data reweighting learns which observations to down-weight, improving robustness when probabilistic modeling assumptions mismatch the data.

paragraphs: This paper develops an expectation propagation method for Gaussian process classification with multiple classes and very large datasets. The key computational feature is an estimated log marginal likelihood expressed as a sum over observations. That structure supports stochastic-gradient training with mini-batches, so each training update can work with a subset of the data.

With this training scheme, the computation for an update does not depend on the total number of observations. Additional assumptions in approximate inference also make memory requirements independent of that total. These changes allow the proposed method to operate on datasets containing millions of examples while using the stated approximation framework.

Empirical comparisons with variational inference approaches show similar or better performance. Some alternatives yield significantly worse predictive distributions as measured by test log likelihood. The proposed method also appears to converge in fewer training iterations. These findings support its practical combination of scalable training and predictive quality, while the iteration advantage is presented as an empirical observation.
icml-2017-scalable-multi-class-gaussian-.tldr: Mini-batch expectation propagation enables multiclass Gaussian process classification on millions of observations with competitive predictive distributions.

paragraphs: Many sequences contain meaningful chunks, such as phrases within language, but their boundaries may be unknown. This paper builds a probabilistic sequence model around that segmental structure. For a particular segmentation, it calculates the sequence probability by multiplying the probabilities of its segments, which can be modeled using tools such as recurrent neural networks.

Rather than fixing one segmentation in advance, the model sums over all valid segmentations to obtain the sequence's probability. This incorporates uncertainty about where boundaries belong directly into the calculation. The authors develop efficient dynamic programming for both forward and backward computations, carrying out these operations without approximation.

The approach is demonstrated on text segmentation and speech recognition. Alongside quantitative results, the authors show that it can discover segments that are meaningful within those applications. The contribution is a way to combine flexible models of individual segments with exact computation over possible segmentations, making chunk structure part of the sequence model itself.
icml-2017-sequence-modeling-via-segmenta.tldr: A probabilistic sequence model uses exact dynamic programming to account for unknown segment boundaries and discover meaningful chunks.

paragraphs: Sketching reduces the computational size of a regression problem, but a good approximation to its optimization objective need not preserve its statistical behavior. This paper examines that distinction for matrix ridge regression, comparing classical sketching with Hessian sketching. Regularization makes the statistical effects different from those previously studied for ordinary least squares.

Classical sketching recovers nearly optimal objective values, whereas Hessian sketching lacks that guarantee; its approximation error depends on the response mass and optimal objective value. Statistical bounds reveal another contrast: classical sketches substantially increase variance, while Hessian sketches substantially increase bias. Ridge regression therefore introduces a bias-variance tradeoff absent from the sketched least-squares setting discussed.

Experiments show that sketched solutions can have statistical risks an order of magnitude above those of optimal ridge solutions. The authors establish theoretically and empirically that averaging models greatly reduces this gap. In distributed settings, sketching with model averaging thus offers a way to obtain near-optimal solutions quickly while mitigating the statistical costs of sketching.
icml-2017-sketched-ridge-regression-opti.tldr: Sketching can increase ridge regression's bias or variance, while model averaging substantially reduces the resulting statistical risk.

paragraphs: Tensor decomposition is used across several disciplines, and the tensor power method is a common approach to the problem. Earlier theoretically guaranteed versions recover leading eigenvectors one at a time. This paper addresses whether those eigenvectors can instead be found simultaneously, bringing a capability available for matrices into the tensor setting.

The central contribution is a new initialization procedure that enables simultaneous recovery through power iteration. Initialization is therefore a key part of the change in how the decomposition is computed. The method moves from a sequence of individual eigenvector searches to a procedure that finds multiple eigenvectors together, with theoretical support for that approach.

The authors report two resulting improvements: better running time when working with a batch of data and lower sample complexity when processing data in a streaming setting. These address distinct resources, computation in one case and required observations in the other. The work shows how changing initialization and recovery together can improve both aspects of tensor decomposition.
icml-2017-tensor-decomposition-via-simul.tldr: A new initialization enables simultaneous tensor eigenvector recovery, improving batch running time and streaming sample complexity.

paragraphs: Temporal point processes model sequences of events, including activities generated by online users. This paper moves from describing such events to controlling a stochastic system driven by them. The objective is to design a policy that guides the system toward a target state despite randomness in when events occur.

The authors approach stochastic optimal control through optimal measures and variational inference. This perspective leads to a convex optimization framework and an efficient algorithm for adapting the policy to the current system state. State-dependent updates matter because the policy can respond to the system as it evolves while pursuing the specified target.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show more accurate and efficient steering of user activities than the other stochastic control methods considered. The contribution connects probabilistic reasoning about event sequences with adaptive policy design. Its reported benefits concern both how closely the system reaches the desired behavior and how efficiently the control procedure operates.
icml-2017-variational-policy-for-guiding.tldr: A variational, convex optimization framework adapts control policies to steer point-process-driven systems toward target states.
